methodological_rigor.justification: Single-center retrospective study of 74 HCC patients post-MWA with a reasonable dual analytic strategy (paired intra-group and between-group comparisons), a reference standard adjudicated by a 3-physician expert committee with follow-up confirmation, and blinded independent readers (5 and 10 years' experience). However, MRI allocation was explicitly non-random and skewed toward high-risk/ambiguous patients, and the authors acknowledge this creates intrinsic bias favoring MRI. No sample-size justification, no verification bias adjustment, no sensitivity analysis, and only 20 recurrences in the CT+MRI group limit precision for paired diagnostic metrics.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: The findings reinforce the role of Gd-EOB-DTPA MRI as an adjunctive surveillance tool post-MWA and produced BCLC upstaging in 2/20 (10%) patients, with practical implications for salvage therapy selection. However, the selection bias toward high-risk patients and single-center retrospective design limits direct translational claims; the authors appropriately position MRI as an adjunct rather than replacement. Design is a retrospective diagnostic accuracy study with non-random comparator allocation, best classified as Oxford LoE 3b.

reporting_quality.justification: Many STARD elements are addressed (eligibility criteria, reference standard definition, blinding, test parameters, inter-observer kappa, AUROC with DeLong), and the Results section reports patient-based and lesion-based metrics with kappa. However, there is no explicit STARD checklist, no flow diagram description, confidence intervals for sensitivities/specificities are promised but not shown in the text, and no data/code availability statement. The manuscript layout has the Results section placed under "Additional Sections" after the Discussion, a structural irregularity.

novelty_literature.justification: The superiority of Gd-EOB-DTPA-enhanced MRI over CECT for HCC lesion detection, particularly sub-2 cm lesions, is already established by multiple meta-analyses (Guo 2016, Li 2019, Liu 2017) and a prospective study by Imai et al. in the post-RFA setting. This work extends the evidence slightly to the post-MWA setting but does not introduce new diagnostic criteria, novel imaging techniques, or mechanistic insight.

writing_presentation.justification: The manuscript is generally readable with clear methods descriptions and an informative illustrative case in Figure 1. However, the unconventional placement of the Results section after the Discussion under "Additional Sections" disrupts readability. There is also redundancy in the discussion of HBP hypointensity and DWI literature, and some long sentences could be tightened.

key_strengths: Blinded independent reader study with Cohen's kappa (0.84 MRI, 0.70-0.58 CT) and a committee-based reference standard with imaging follow-up confirmation
Both patient-based and lesion-based diagnostic metrics with DeLong AUROC comparisons reported
Authors explicitly acknowledge non-random MRI allocation and appropriately position MRI as an adjunct for high-risk or equivocal CT findings
Clinically actionable observation that BCLC upstaging occurred in 10% of CT+MRI patients with additional <=1.5 cm lesions detected
key_concerns: Selection bias: MRI performed only in high-risk/equivocal-CT patients intrinsically favors MRI in comparative analyses
Small single-center sample (n=74, only 20 CT+MRI recurrences) limits statistical precision and generalizability
Incremental novelty; diagnostic superiority of EOB-MRI is well established in prior meta-analyses cited in the manuscript
Unusual manuscript structure (Results placed after Discussion) and no STARD checklist or flow diagram
No data/code availability statement; 95% CIs for diagnostic metrics promised in statistical methods are not reported in the provided text
chief_reviewer.rationale: Methodologically competent but biased and incremental single-center diagnostic study; appropriate for a mid-tier radiology or oncology journal after major revisions addressing structure, STARD reporting, and selection bias.
